classification_signals: This is a doctoral dissertation comprising multiple empirical studies.
The thesis describes four distinct studies (Study 1, 2A, 2B, 3, 4) with detailed methods, participants, measures, and results sections (Chapter 3, p. 62-88).
Studies 1 and 2 utilized computer simulations (Lightscape) to manipulate lighting conditions (p. 64, 69).
Studies 3 and 4 were field experiments conducted in real-world suburban environments (p. 75, 85).
Statistical analyses include repeated measures ANOVA and linear correlation (p. 66, 70, 80, 86).
Participants evaluated scenes/areas using questionnaires with Likert scales (p. 65, 69, 73, 79).

limitations: Research on restoration is limited to perceived restorativeness, not behavioral and/or physiological levels (p. 97).
Small sample of settings limits generalizability to all scene contents and environmental contexts (p. 97).
Reliability of explorative field studies 3 and 4 is questioned due to numerous confounded factors, single-item scales, and small sample sizes (p. 97).
Studies 1 and 2 used simulations instead of real environments, and the Lightscape simulations were rather coarse (p. 97).
The absence of sound in simulations may overemphasize the effect of the visual environment, especially for fear ratings (p. 98).
Time of day and season may affect lighting preferences; studies 1 and 2 were conducted during daytime for night-time environments (p. 98).
Single-item scales used in studies 3 and 4 may harm the reliability of the results (p. 98).
The use of local residents in studies 3 and 4 is a potential source of bias (p. 98).
Cultural differences in lighting preferences need more attention (p. 99).
The use of outdoor lighting is mainly restricted to colder seasons in Finland, and perceptions may differ in different climate zones (p. 99).
Nonlinear brightness and extensiveness scales may have confused participants (p. 99).
The salience of the stimuli used; eye tracking and luminance measurements in real environments are needed (p. 99).
minimum_safe_summary: This doctoral dissertation investigates how lighting influences perceptions of restorativeness, preference, and fear in outdoor spaces, integrating environmental psychology and lighting technology. Across multiple empirical studies, including simulations and field experiments, findings indicate that focusing light on natural elements enhances perceived restorativeness, preference, and safety, while urban elements have the opposite effect. Perceived color quality emerged as a strong predictor of both safety and pleasantness. The research highlights that excessive brightness and glare can negatively impact restorative experiences, suggesting that quality-based lighting approaches, rather than merely increasing illuminance, are crucial for creating pleasant and safe near-home nightscapes. Limitations include the focus on perceived rather than physiological restoration, the use of simulations, small sample sizes in some studies, and potential cultural and contextual biases.
